root.note: Accusative sōlitātem, from sōlus ‘alone’. The change from soidade to saudade is irregular; Wiktionary says it was very likely influenced by saudar ‘to greet’ and by an older saudade ‘salvation’ (from salūtātem).

history: Saudade is often called untranslatable. It is the longing for someone or something you love and do not have, a person far away, a place, a time that is gone, sometimes with a little sweetness in the sadness. The word began as plain loneliness: Latin sōlitātem, from sōlus, ‘alone’. Medieval poets wrote soidade. The vowel then changed in an irregular way, very likely pulled by saudar, ‘to greet’, and the form saudade won. In daily Portuguese it is less solemn than its reputation: tenho saudades tuas means ‘I miss you’, and que saudades! is ‘I've missed this!’. Galician kept a form closer to the Latin, soidade.
historyEinfach: Saudade is a famous Portuguese word. It means missing someone or something you love: a person, a place, a time. The word comes from Latin and first meant ‘loneliness’. In everyday Portuguese you say tenho saudades tuas: ‘I miss you’.

elsewhere.text: Spanish kept the same Latin word with its first meaning: loneliness.
English solitude comes from a sister word built on the same sōlus, ‘alone’.
